sections.heading: Title
sections.text: Soft tree ensembles are gradient-trained decision trees that rival neural networks on tabular data, yet their training behavior has lacked theoretical grounding. This paper, presented at ICLR 2022, introduces the Tree Neural Tangent Kernel, or TNTK, which describes an ensemble of infinitely many soft trees. Using the TNTK, the authors prove global convergence of training, show that oblivious tree structures are equivalent to ordinary ones in this limit, and reveal that very deep trees suffer a degeneracy that flattens the kernel. The theory is validated on ninety real-world datasets and explains empirical tricks practitioners already rely on.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.text: Tree ensembles and neural networks are two of the most widely used model families in machine learning. A soft tree is a variant of a decision tree whose splitting rules are made differentiable, so the whole model can be trained by gradient descent instead of a greedy search. Ensembles of soft trees perform very well, especially on tabular datasets, and practitioners have accumulated many training techniques such as parameter sharing, adjusting split hardness, and over-parameterization. Yet almost no theoretical work explains why these models and their training tricks work. This paper sets out to fill that gap.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: The Neural Tangent Kernel has become a powerful tool for understanding neural networks with infinitely many hidden nodes. It has been derived for multi-layer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and many other architectures, and each architecture produces its own distinct kernel. But no one had derived an NTK for tree ensembles. Because soft trees inherit characteristics of neural networks, the authors recognized that the NTK framework was the natural lens for analyzing them. The motivation is to obtain, for the first time, a closed-form kernel that captures the behavior of an ensemble of infinitely many soft trees.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: The paper makes four main contributions. First, it derives the Tree Neural Tangent Kernel at initialization for an ensemble of infinitely many perfect binary trees of arbitrary depth, and proves the kernel remains essentially constant during training, which lets the authors analyze learning as kernel regression and establish global convergence. Second, it proves that oblivious tree ensembles, where splitting rules are shared within each depth as in the NODE model, converge to the very same kernel as non-oblivious trees. Third, it characterizes the decision function, showing the kernel is nearly linear in the basic case and becomes nonlinear as splits are made harder. Fourth, it uncovers a degeneracy phenomenon in which the kernel of deep trees becomes almost constant, explaining why very deep soft trees generalize poorly.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: The method begins by taking the number of trees to infinity. For an ensemble of perfect binary soft trees of depth d, the authors prove that the Tree Neural Tangent Kernel converges in probability to a deterministic kernel. This kernel has two interpretable pieces: a contribution from the inner splitting nodes and a contribution from the leaves. The soft splitting operation uses a scaled error function, essentially a smooth sigmoid, whose sharpness is set by a scaling parameter alpha. Crucially, the split expectations have closed-form expressions, so the whole kernel is available analytically. Because the kernel stays constant throughout gradient training and is positive definite, training reduces to kernel regression and is guaranteed to converge globally. And because the formula is not recursive in depth, computing the kernel costs the same no matter how deep the trees are.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.text: The empirical study uses two kinds of data. For generalization, the authors run kernel regression with the Tree Neural Tangent Kernel on ninety real-world datasets and compare it against the kernel induced by an infinitely wide multi-layer perceptron and against the classic radial basis function kernel. Tree depth is tuned from one up to twenty-nine, and the split-hardness parameter alpha is swept across a wide range. For measuring computational cost, they use a synthetic dataset of three hundred samples with ten Gaussian features. Additional synthetic experiments confirm that the finite-tree kernel converges to the theoretical infinite-tree kernel and that training dynamics match the kernel-regression prediction.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.text: The experiments confirm every theoretical prediction. As the number of trees grows, the empirical kernel converges to the closed-form Tree Neural Tangent Kernel, and the observed output dynamics of training match what kernel regression predicts. When trees are made deeper, accuracy first improves and then deteriorates, exactly the degeneracy the theory anticipates. On the ninety real-world datasets, the multi-layer perceptron kernel wins on average, but the tree kernel is actually better on more than thirty percent of individual datasets, where the tree inductive bias fits the data. And because the tree kernel's cost does not grow with depth, it is dramatically faster to compute than the MLP kernel as depth increases.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: Two ablations are central. Sweeping the split-hardness parameter alpha shows a clear trend: harder splits give better dataset-wise win rates against the MLP kernel, climbing from about fourteen percent when splits are soft to nearly thirty-five percent at the hardest setting, all well above the radial basis function baseline. Sweeping tree depth reproduces the degeneracy story, with accuracy first improving and then declining as trees get deeper. The authors also verify their oblivious-tree theorem empirically, confirming that the parameter-sharing structure used by models like NODE induces the same kernel as ordinary soft trees in the infinite limit.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.text: A few numbers capture the impact. Across ninety real-world datasets, the tree kernel outperforms the multi-layer perceptron kernel on more than thirty percent of them, with a peak dataset-wise win rate of about thirty-five percent when splits are hard, compared to under twelve percent for the radial basis function kernel. Perhaps most striking, the computational cost of the tree kernel does not depend on tree depth at all, whereas the multi-layer perceptron kernel scales linearly with depth. The study spans tree depths from one to twenty-nine.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.text: The lasting takeaway is that the neural tangent kernel framework, previously used only for neural networks, can be applied to tree models. The resulting Tree Neural Tangent Kernel explains a range of soft-tree behaviors from a single theory: training converges globally, oblivious parameter sharing costs nothing in the infinite limit, deep trees degenerate into a nearly constant kernel, and harder splitting functions produce a more useful nonlinear kernel. Along the way it delivers a practical kernel whose cost is independent of depth, making it an attractive, fast alternative to the multi-layer perceptron kernel on tabular data.
